title: Probability paradoxes: Monty Hall, the birthday problem, and more
description: Monty Hall, the birthday paradox, the gambler's fallacy, and other puzzles where the math disagrees with your gut. Each question offers a tempting wrong answer, and each explanation teaches the rule behind the right one: independence, conditional probability, expected value, or the complement trick. Every explanation links to a source for further reading.
author: Quizbun

questions.title: What range of numbers can a probability take?

options.text: From `0` to `1`, where `0` means impossible and `1` means certain
From `-1` to `1`, where `-1` means impossible
From `0` to `100` only, never a fraction
Any real number, where a larger value just means more likely

questions.explanation: A probability is a number from `0` to `1`. `0` means the event can't happen, `1` means it's certain, and the values in between say how likely it is. The probabilities of all possible outcomes add up to `1`. A percentage like 25% is the same number multiplied by 100, so it stays between 0% and 100%. Keep this range in mind and you can throw out any answer that comes out negative or above 1.

questions.title: A weather model gives a 30% chance of rain tomorrow. What is the chance of no rain?

options.text: It cannot be determined from this

questions.explanation: Either it rains or it doesn't, so the two probabilities add up to `1`. That's the complement rule: `P(no rain) = 1 - P(rain) = 1 - 0.30 = 0.70`. Working out the easier opposite and subtracting it from 1 is one of the most useful tricks in probability. You'll use it again for the birthday paradox later in this quiz.

questions.title: When every outcome in the sample space is equally likely, how do you find the probability of an event?
questions.description: The *sample space* is the set of all possible outcomes of the experiment.

options.text: Favourable outcomes divided by the total number of possible outcomes
Favourable outcomes multiplied by the total number of outcomes
Total outcomes divided by favourable outcomes
Always one half, by symmetry

questions.explanation: This is the classical definition: `P(event) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes`. On a fair die, `P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2`. The formula only works when the outcomes really are equally likely. Several paradoxes in this quiz trip people up by quietly breaking that condition.

questions.title: You roll two fair six-sided dice and add them. Which total is the most likely?

options.text: Every total from 2 to 12 is equally likely

questions.explanation: Two dice give 36 equally likely ordered pairs. Six of them add up to 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), and (6,1). That makes `P(7) = 6/36 = 1/6`, higher than any other total. A 2 or a 12 can each happen only one way, so each has `1/36`. The mistake is treating the 11 possible totals as equally likely. What counts is how many pairs produce each total.

questions.title: Two events are independent. How do you find the probability that both happen?
questions.description: *Independent* means the outcome of one event tells you nothing about the other.

options.text: Multiply their probabilities
Add their probabilities
Subtract the smaller from the larger
Take the average of the two

questions.explanation: For independent events, `P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)`. Two fair coins both landing heads: `1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4`. Adding would be wrong, and the sum could even go above 1. This multiplication rule comes back twice later: it explains why 23 people are enough for a likely shared birthday, and it's exactly what the gambler's fallacy forgets.

questions.title: On one roll of a fair die, what is the probability of rolling a 1 or a 2?
questions.explanation: A single roll can't be both a 1 and a 2, so the two events are *mutually exclusive* and you can add them: `P(1 or 2) = 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3`. Simple addition only works when the events can't overlap. If they can both happen, subtract the overlap so you don't count it twice: `P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)`.

questions.title: What does the conditional probability P(A | B) measure?

options.text: The probability of A, given that B has already occurred
The probability that A causes B
The probability of A and B happening in either order
The probability of A plus the probability of B

questions.explanation: Conditional probability is the chance of A once you know B happened: `P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B)`. New information can change the odds a lot. Seeing the host open a goat door in Monty Hall, or getting a positive result on a medical test, are two examples later in this quiz. When A and B are independent, knowing B changes nothing, so `P(A | B) = P(A)`.

questions.title: What is the expected (average) value of one roll of a fair six-sided die?
questions.explanation: To get the expected value, multiply each outcome by its probability and add them up: `(1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) / 6 = 21/6 = 3.5`. No die shows 3.5. Expected value is the average over many rolls, not a prediction for any single one. The roulette question at the end uses the same tool to show why casino bets lose money over time.

questions.title: You roll one die four times. Is getting at least one six more likely than not?
questions.description: This 17th-century gambling puzzle helped launch probability theory.

options.text: Yes, about 51.8%, slightly in the bettor's favour
No, it is exactly 4/6, so 66.7%
No, it is exactly 50%, a perfectly fair bet
Yes, about 90%, almost guaranteed

questions.explanation: Adding four chances of `1/6` counts the overlaps twice. Use the complement instead: `P(no six in 4 rolls) = (5/6)^4 ≈ 0.482`, so `P(at least one six) = 1 - 0.482 ≈ 0.518`. The gambler Chevalier de Méré also bet on getting at least one double six in 24 throws of two dice, and he kept losing. That bet works out to `1 - (35/36)^24 ≈ 0.491`, just under half. He couldn't see why two similar bets landed on opposite sides of 50%, and his question led to the 1654 letters between Pascal and Fermat that founded probability theory.

questions.title: A fair coin has landed heads five times in a row. What is the probability the next flip is heads?

options.text: Much less than 1/2, because tails is now overdue
Much more than 1/2, because heads is clearly hot

questions.explanation: Each flip is independent, so the next one is `1/2` whatever came before. The coin doesn't remember. Six heads in a row from the start does have probability `(1/2)^6 = 1/64`, but five of those heads have already happened. Only the sixth flip is still open, and it's 50/50. Believing tails is "due" is the gambler's fallacy.

questions.title: Which belief is the gambler's fallacy?

options.text: That past independent outcomes change the odds of future ones, so a result becomes "due"
That the house always has a mathematical edge
That genuinely rare events can never happen
That every outcome in a game is equally likely

questions.explanation: The gambler's fallacy, also called the Monte Carlo fallacy, is the belief that a streak of one outcome makes the opposite outcome more likely next time, even though the events are *independent*. A roulette wheel or a coin doesn't remember past results or try to balance them. One of the wrong answers, the house edge, is real: casinos do have a long-run advantage. Telling real edges apart from imagined corrections is the point of this question.

questions.title: Why doesn't a streak of heads make tails more likely on the next flip?

options.text: Flips are independent, and the coin keeps no record of past results
The coin is secretly biased toward heads
The law of large numbers forces an immediate correction
Five heads in a row is impossible, so the data must be wrong

questions.explanation: A coin carries nothing over from one toss to the next, so every flip has the same 50/50 odds. The law of large numbers does pull the share of heads toward `1/2` over time. It does this slowly, as many new flips dilute the early streak. It never makes one particular flip more likely to land tails.

questions.title: At the Monte Carlo Casino in 1913, the roulette ball reportedly landed on black 26 times in a row. What happened next?

options.text: Gamblers lost huge sums betting on red, sure it was "due"
A payout bug bankrupted the casino
Someone proved the wheel had been rigged
Mathematicians revised the laws of probability

questions.explanation: This 1913 run is where the gambler's fallacy got its other name, the Monte Carlo fallacy. As black kept coming up, players bet more and more on red, sure the streak had to end. They lost fortunes, because every spin was independent. For a 50/50 game, a specific run of 26 has probability `(1/2)^26`, about 1 in 67 million. That's very unlikely before it starts, but once the streak is underway, red is still no more likely on the next spin.

questions.title: What does the law of large numbers actually promise about flipping a fair coin?

options.text: The proportion of heads gets closer to 1/2 as the number of flips grows
The number of heads and tails becomes exactly equal
Any long streak will soon be cancelled by an opposite streak
After enough flips, heads and tails start to alternate

questions.explanation: The law of large numbers says the *proportion* of heads approaches the true probability, `1/2`, as you flip more. It doesn't promise equal counts, and it doesn't promise that one streak gets cancelled by another. People often cite it to defend the gambler's fallacy. The proportion settles because later flips outnumber the early imbalance, not because the coin pays back a debt.

questions.title: As you keep flipping a fair coin, what happens to the raw gap between the number of heads and the number of tails?
questions.description: The *proportion* of heads moves toward 1/2. This question asks about the absolute difference between the two counts.

options.text: It tends to grow, roughly with the square root of n, even as the proportion evens out
It steadily shrinks to zero
It stays fixed once a streak ends
It swings neatly between +1 and -1

questions.explanation: This is why the gambler's fallacy fails. The proportion of heads approaches `1/2`, but the gap `|heads - tails|` usually *grows*, roughly like `sqrt(n)`. That's a standard result about random walks. No corrective streak ever evens out the counts. An early surplus stays, but it becomes a smaller and smaller fraction of the total as you keep flipping.

questions.title: Someone walks in, sees you roll a double six, and says, "You must have been rolling for a long time to finally get that." What mistake is this?

options.text: The inverse gambler's fallacy: one independent roll says nothing about how many came before
The base-rate fallacy
Simpson's paradox
A perfectly correct Bayesian inference

questions.explanation: The philosopher Ian Hacking named this the inverse gambler's fallacy. It reasons backwards, treating a rare result as proof that many attempts came first. Each roll is independent, so seeing a double six tells you nothing about how many rolls came before it. A double six is as likely on the first roll as on the thousandth.

questions.title: The gambler's fallacy expects a streak to reverse. Which belief expects a streak to continue?

options.text: The hot-hand belief
The Monte Carlo fallacy
The law of averages
The maturity of chances

questions.explanation: The hot-hand belief is the opposite of the gambler's fallacy. After a run of successes it expects more of the same ("she's on fire"), while the gambler's fallacy expects a reversal ("a miss is due"). For truly independent events, both are wrong. The other three answers are all folk names for the gambler's fallacy itself. Whether a real hot hand exists in sports is still debated: a well-known 1985 study found none, but a 2018 reanalysis found a statistical bias in that study and reopened the question.

questions.title: Monty Hall: three doors hide a car and two goats. You pick a door. The host, who knows where the car is, opens a different door to show a goat and offers you the chance to switch. Should you?

options.text: Yes, switching wins about 2/3 of the time
It makes no difference, it's now 50/50
No, staying wins about 2/3 of the time
Switch only if you originally guessed wrong

questions.explanation: Switching wins `2/3` of the time, and staying wins `1/3`. Your first pick is right only `1/3` of the time, so `2/3` of the time the car is behind one of the other two doors. The host must open a goat door from those two, so the whole `2/3` moves to the one door he leaves closed. The 50/50 answer feels right because it ignores that the host doesn't choose at random.

questions.title: In the standard Monty Hall game, what makes switching better than staying?

options.text: The host knows where the car is and always opens a goat door on purpose
The car is more likely to be behind a higher-numbered door
The contestant's first pick is psychologically biased
There is no real reason, it's just a trick of the mind

questions.explanation: It all comes down to what the host knows. He never opens the car door and never opens yours, so the door he leaves shut gets the combined `2/3` probability of the two doors you didn't pick. His choice gives you information, and you update your odds using Bayes' rule. If he opened a door at random, the advantage would disappear, as the next question shows.

questions.title: The 2/3 advantage for switching depends on how the host behaves. Which rules does it need?

options.text: The host always opens a goat door, never your door, and always offers the switch
The host opens a door at random, sometimes revealing the car
The host offers a switch only when you have already picked the car
No rules are needed, 2/3 holds however the host behaves

questions.explanation: The `2/3` answer needs a host who always shows a goat, never opens your door, and always offers the switch. Change the rules and the answer changes. A "Monty from Hell" who offers a switch only when you've already picked the car would make switching lose every time. Spelling out these rules is what turned a famous "paradox" into a solved problem.

questions.title: Now imagine 100 doors. You pick one, and the host opens 98 of the others, all goats, leaving one door closed. Should you switch?

options.text: Yes, the remaining door wins about 99% of the time
No difference, it's now 50/50
No, your original door is now 99% likely
Switching wins exactly half the time

questions.explanation: With 100 doors the logic is easier to see. Your first pick had a `1/100` chance. The host knowingly opens 98 goat doors among the other 99, so their combined `99/100` chance goes to the one door he leaves shut. Switching wins 99 times out of 100. If the 50/50 answer still feels right with three doors, try picturing 100.

questions.title: Variant: the host forgets where the car is and opens one of the other two doors at random. It happens to show a goat. Should you switch now?

options.text: It no longer matters, switching and staying both win 1/2 of the time
Switching still wins 2/3
Staying now wins 2/3
Switching wins 99/100

questions.explanation: Jeffrey Rosenthal analysed this "Monty Fall" variant. When the host opens a door by accident, the fact that it showed a goat raises the odds of both closed doors equally, so each ends up at `1/2`. The `2/3` advantage in the original game comes from the host's knowledge, not from seeing a goat. The doors look the same in both versions, but the answer is different.

questions.title: When Marilyn vos Savant published the "switch" answer in Parade magazine in 1990, how did readers react?

options.text: Thousands wrote in to say she was wrong, many of them with advanced degrees
Everyone accepted it right away
Nobody noticed it until the 2000s
Casinos sued her for revealing a betting secret

questions.explanation: vos Savant said to switch for a `2/3` chance of winning. She got about 10,000 letters, many from mathematicians and PhDs, telling her she was wrong. She was right. The mathematician Paul Erdős reportedly stayed unconvinced until someone showed him a computer simulation. It's still one of the best examples of a simple, correct answer that almost everyone's intuition rejects.

questions.title: Where did the Monty Hall problem first appear in print in its game-show form?

options.text: A 1975 letter by Steve Selvin in the journal The American Statistician
Marilyn vos Savant invented it from scratch in 1990
A 1950s textbook written by the host Monty Hall himself
Blaise Pascal first posed it in the 1650s

questions.explanation: The statistician Steve Selvin posed and solved the puzzle in a 1975 letter to *The American Statistician*, naming it after Monty Hall, the host of *Let's Make a Deal*. Mathematically it's close to Bertrand's box paradox from 1889. vos Savant made it world-famous in 1990, but she didn't invent it.

questions.title: How many people need to be in a room before it's more likely than not that two of them share a birthday?
questions.description: Ignore leap years, and assume birthdays are spread evenly across 365 days.

options.text: Just 23
183, about half of 365

questions.explanation: With just 23 people, the chance of at least one shared birthday is about `50.7%`. The popular guess of about 183, half of 365, answers a different question. "Does someone share *my* birthday?" is not the same as "Do *any two* people share a birthday?" The next few questions explain why 23 is enough.

questions.title: Why are just 23 people enough to make a shared birthday likely?

options.text: What matters is the number of pairs, and 23 people form 253 pairs
Most people happen to be born in the same few months
23 is more than half of the 52 weeks in a year
Human birthdays are not actually random

questions.explanation: A shared birthday needs a matching *pair*, and the number of pairs grows much faster than the number of people. Twenty-three people make `C(23,2) = (23 × 22) / 2 = 253` pairs. With 253 chances, each about `1/365`, a match becomes more likely than not. Once you count pairs instead of people, the paradox goes away.

questions.title: What's the easiest way to calculate the probability of at least one shared birthday?

options.text: Find the probability that all birthdays are different, then subtract it from 1
Add 1/365 once for every person in the room
Multiply 1/365 by the number of people
Divide the number of people by 365

questions.explanation: Counting every way a match can happen means handling lots of overlaps. The complement is much easier: `P(all different) = (365/365) × (364/365) × (363/365) × ...`, since each new person has to avoid the birthdays already taken. Then `P(at least one match) = 1 - P(all different)`, which is about `0.507` for 23 people. Adding `1/365` per person ignores the overlaps, and in a big enough room it would give an answer above 1.

questions.title: In a room of 70 people, roughly how likely is it that two share a birthday?

options.text: About 99.9%, practically certain
About 70%
About 50%
About 19%, roughly 70 out of 365

questions.explanation: The chance rises fast: about `50.7%` at 23 people, about `97%` at 50, and about `99.9%` at 70. That's nearly certain, long before you reach the 366 people you'd need to guarantee it. The number of pairs, and with it the chance of a match, grows much faster than the number of people.

questions.title: Ignoring leap years, so there are 365 possible birthdays, how many people guarantee that two of them share a birthday?

options.text: It can never be made 100% certain

questions.explanation: This is the pigeonhole principle. With only 365 possible birthdays, 366 people can't all have different ones, so a shared birthday is guaranteed. If you count February 29 as a possible day, you need 367. The surprise of the paradox is the distance between a certain match at 366 people and a likely one at just 23.

questions.title: How many other people need to be in a room before there's a better-than-even chance that someone shares your birthday?

options.text: About 253
About 23
About 183
About 365

questions.explanation: This is the question most people *think* the birthday paradox asks, and the answer is very different. Matching one fixed date is much harder than finding any match. You need `(364/365)^n` to fall below `0.5`, which first happens at `n = 253`. Compare the two numbers: 253 people for someone to share *your* birthday, and just 23 for *any two* people to match.

questions.title: The "birthday attack" in cryptography uses the same math. Roughly how many random items do you need to generate before you're likely to find a collision among N equally likely hash values?

options.text: About the square root of N
About N
About N divided by 2
About N squared

questions.explanation: Collisions show up after about `sqrt(N)` tries, not `N`. A hash with `2^n` possible outputs will likely produce a collision after about `2^(n/2)` attempts. That's why a 128-bit hash gives only about 64 bits of *collision* resistance. Pairs add up quickly in a room of 23 people, and they add up just as quickly among hash outputs, so collisions are much cheaper to find than most people expect.

questions.title: A disease affects 1% of people. A test is 99% accurate for both sick and healthy people. You test positive. What's the chance you actually have the disease?
questions.description: Many doctors get this one wrong.

options.text: About 50%
About 99%
About 1%
About 98%

questions.explanation: Picture 10,000 people. About 100 are sick, and 99 of them test positive. About 9,900 are healthy, and 1% of them, about 99 people, also test positive. That's about 198 positive results, and only half come from sick people: `99 / 198 = 50%`. The disease is rare, so false positives from the large healthy group are as common as true positives. Forgetting how rare the disease is, its base rate, is called the base-rate fallacy. The math behind it is Bayes' theorem.

questions.title: Linda is 31, single, outspoken, and studied philosophy. She cares deeply about social justice. Which is more probable?

options.text: Linda is a bank teller
Linda is a bank teller who is also active in the feminist movement
The two statements are exactly equally probable
There is not enough information to compare them

questions.explanation: This is Tversky and Kahneman's Linda problem. Two things together can never be more likely than one of them alone. Every feminist bank teller *is* a bank teller, so `P(bank teller) ≥ P(bank teller AND feminist)`. The description fits the feminist option so well that most people rank it higher anyway. That mistake is called the conjunction fallacy.

questions.title: What is Simpson's paradox?

options.text: A trend that appears within several groups can reverse when the groups are combined
A rare event becomes certain if you wait long enough
Two independent events that only seem to be dependent
The average of the averages always equals the overall average

questions.explanation: In Simpson's paradox, combining groups of data can flip the direction of an effect. The classic example is UC Berkeley's 1973 graduate admissions. Overall, the numbers looked biased against women. Yet in most departments, women were admitted at the same rate as men or higher. Women had applied more often to the most competitive departments, and that caused the reversal. Splitting or combining the data can reverse the conclusion, so choose the grouping carefully.

questions.title: A family has two children. You learn that at least one is a boy, but not which one. If boys and girls are equally likely and independent, what's the probability that both are boys?
questions.explanation: List the equally likely birth orders: BB, BG, GB, GG. "At least one boy" rules out only GG, which leaves BB, BG, and GB. Only one of those three is two boys, so the answer is `1/3`. If you'd been told "the *older* child is a boy", the answer would be `1/2`. The two statements sound almost the same but give you different information, and that's why this paradox is famous.

questions.title: In many real-world datasets, like populations, street addresses, and financial figures, how often is the first digit a 1?

options.text: About 30%, far more often than the 11% you might expect
About 11.1%, because every digit from 1 to 9 is equally likely
Exactly 10%
About 50%

questions.explanation: Benford's law says the first digit `d` appears with probability `log10(1 + 1/d)`. So 1 comes first about `30.1%` of the time, and 9 only about `4.6%`, not the even `11.1%` you might guess. The law tends to hold for data that spans several orders of magnitude. Auditors look for departures from it to catch made-up numbers in accounting and possible election fraud.

questions.title: A game: flip a fair coin until it lands heads. If the first head comes on flip k, you win 2^k dollars. What's the expected payout?

options.text: Infinite, yet almost no one would pay much to play
Exactly $2
Exactly $4
Zero

questions.explanation: Each possible flip adds `(1/2^k) × 2^k = 1` dollar to the expected value, and there are infinitely many flips, so the total is `1 + 1 + 1 + ... = infinity`. Still, almost nobody would pay more than a few dollars to play. That's the St. Petersburg paradox. Daniel Bernoulli resolved it in 1738 with the idea of expected *utility*: each extra dollar matters less to you than the one before, so the game is worth a finite, sensible price. The puzzle helped found modern decision theory.

questions.title: On an American roulette wheel with 38 pockets, you bet $1 on a single number, which pays 35 to 1. What do you expect to win or lose per $1 bet in the long run?

options.text: Lose about 5.3 cents, the house edge
Break even on average
Win about 5.3 cents
Lose exactly 50 cents

questions.explanation: The expected value is `(1/38)(+$35) + (37/38)(-$1) = -$2/38 ≈ -$0.053`, a `5.26%` house edge. A fair payout would be 37 to 1, not 35 to 1, and the casino keeps the difference. No betting system changes this average, and neither does waiting for a number that's "due" (that's the gambler's fallacy). The edge is built into the payout. A European wheel has 37 pockets with a single zero, which cuts the edge to about `2.7%`.
